newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AGROKHLEB - Ukraine livestock decline to continue.
newsitem.headline: AGROKHLEB - Ukraine livestock decline to continue.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from SovEcon Ltd, an independent research organisation specialising in agricultural production and trade in the former Soviet Union, in association with Ukragroconsult, a private Ukrainian agricultural consultancy based in Kiev.
MOSCOW, April 30 - Ukraine's livestock sector is still in steep decline and is likely to continue to fall in 1997.
Total cattle inventories as of April 1 were around 14 percent down on the same year-ago levels, with pig numbers down by 21 percent. The decline is true both of public and private sectors.
Meat and milk output dropped by two and 21 percent respectively during the first four months of the year.
Declines in meat production were registered in 20 out of 25 regions of the country, with the most significant falls in Chernovtzi (31 percent), Kiev (26 percent), and Kherson (22 percent) regions.
There was some increase in meat production in the private sector, but it seems to reflect abnormally high slaughter rates on private plots due to shortages of animal feeds.
Milk output has been falling in all regions, coupled with continued decline in yields per cow.
Despite the continued decline in livestock inventories, feed availability per animal is also falling.
By April 1 availability of all types of feedstuffs had declined to 3.7 million tonnes, of which compound feed accounted for 616,000 tonnes.
This amounts to 0.35 tonnes of total feed per head (as against 0.57 tonnes last year) and 0.06 tonnes of compound feed (against 0.13 tonnes in 1997).
Reduced feed availability was mainly the result of the 1996 crop failure. If the 1997 crop recovers, some increase in feed grain stocks on farms should be seen.
But farmers may well export the bulk of any additional barley they produce, rather than supplying the domestic market to build farm grain stocks.
The decline in livestock numbers in Ukraine therefore seems likely to continue in 1997.
